fade/recall: A recurrent network carries its memory, h, from step to step.
fade/back: Backprop through time sends the gradient back along that chain. Each step back multiplies it by W h h times a tan-aitch slope.
fade/fade: At a half per step, ten steps back shrink it to a half to the tenth: about a thousandth, too little to learn from.
fade/hochreiter: Sepp Hochreiter analyzed this fading in 1991. In 1997, he and Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed a way around it.
fade/cell: Add a second memory, the cell state, c, that skips the weight matrix and the tan-aitch: each step just adds to it.
fade/add: An add gate passes its gradient through unchanged, so along the cell, each step back multiplies by exactly one. Ten steps back, it arrives whole.
fade/name: They called it long short-term memory: LSTM. A network's activations were its short-term memory, its weights the long-term one, and the cell makes the short-term memory last.
gates/gate: The cell's inputs and outputs are run by gates. In backprop, any node of a graph was a gate: an add gate, a multiply gate.
gates/dial: Here the word is narrower: a number from zero to one that multiplies a signal. At one, all of it passes; at zero, none; in between, a share.
gates/sigmoid: A sigmoid makes such a number. Each gate is a sigmoid of the old h and the new x, joined into one vector and weighted, like an RNN step.
gates/cand: The new content is the candidate, g: a tan-aitch of the same inputs, between minus one and one.
gates/input: The input gate, i, scales the candidate before it is added. Near one, the new content goes in; near zero, almost none does.
gates/output: The output gate, o, scales what the cell shows: the new h is o times the tan-aitch of the cell. So the cell can hold a memory without showing it.
forget/grow: That first LSTM never let go: the cell only added, so on a long stream with no marked end, it could grow without limit.
forget/forget: In 2000, Felix Gers, Jürgen Schmidhuber and Fred Cummins added a forget gate, f: a sigmoid that multiplies the old cell. Near one, it keeps the memory; near zero, it lets it go.
forget/formula: So c t equals f t times c t minus one, plus i t times g t: keep a share of the old, write a share of the new.
forget/keep: One unit: the old cell holds two, and the forget gate is zero point three, so it keeps zero point three times two: zero point six.
forget/write: The input gate is zero point eight and the candidate zero point five, so it writes zero point four.
forget/add: The new cell adds the two: zero point six plus zero point four, exactly one.
forget/squash: To show it, the cell goes through a tan-aitch. The tan-aitch of one is about zero point seven six.
forget/show: The output gate is a half, so it lets half of that out: h is about zero point three eight.
forget/layer: A layer does this entry by entry, each unit with its own cell and gates.
path/path: Now the gradient. Along the cell, one step back multiplies it by f: partial c t, partial c t minus one, equals f t. No weight matrix, no tan-aitch slope.
path/lstm: Hold f near one, say at zero point nine five, and twenty steps back still keep about a third of the gradient.
path/rnn: A plain RNN that multiplies by a half at each step keeps one part in a million.
path/learn: The forget gate is learned, so the network can hold it near one for as long as a memory matters.
